normalized.governing_thought: Executive summary: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Grow the software business, which can reach break-even on today’s cash
executive_summary: Answer: No. Parcelbird Now loses money on every combination of inputs seen so far, and it would break the board’s 12-month runway floor even if everything went to plan. Put the cash into the software business instead, including selling fast delivery to grocers, and come back to the operator idea only if the triggers on page 16 are met.
1 The market is growing fast, but nobody is making money from it yet
US quick-commerce GMV grew 42% a year from 2022 to 2025 ($1.8B to $5.1B).
Both incumbents lose money (EBITDA −26% and −46% of revenue). The regional player, QuickBasket, closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.
2 A Parcelbird dark store loses money unless every input beats the best value observed so far
At the 14-site benchmark median a store loses $6.17 per order after site costs. Taking the best observed value for every input still loses $1.76.
The founders’ +$2.02 needs four inputs above anything observed. The Columbus pop-up was below the median on all four, and its customers do not order often enough to repay the $38 acquisition cost.
3 The launch breaks the board’s funding rules even if it goes to plan
Spending $9.5M by month 18 leaves at most $2.5M, about 6 months of today’s burn. The board’s floor is 12 months, or at least $4.8M.
At median economics, nine stores would lose about $18M a year. A one-store pilot (about $3.4M) would breach the floor by month 6.
4 Growing the software business is the better route to profit, and to quick commerce
With $0.8M a year of new hires, the software business breaks even in about 26 months, with cash bottoming out at $5.4M. It stays above the floor as long as ARR grows at least 34% a year.
There are 37 grocers in the pipeline ($3.6M of annual contract value), and several want fast delivery from their own stores, which Parcelbird can sell them as software.
Decisions requested (page 14): turn down the launch and the pilot; approve $0.8M a year of software hires; fund a fast-delivery offer for grocers; adopt the reopening triggers.

We started from the founders’ answer (‘launch’) and tested the four things it needs to be true. None holds in full, so we changed the answer
evidence: Starting hypothesis (the founders’ view): Yes. Launch Parcelbird Now in 2027 with 9 dark stores in 3 cities. Contribution per order turns positive by month 18.

claims.claim: Test 1 Market (~ Half met): Growth is real (42% a year). Profit is not
evidence: both incumbents have negative contribution per order, and the regional one is shrinking

claims.claim: Test 2 Unit economics (✗ Not met): Stores make money only on the founders’ inputs, all of which are above the best value observed
evidence: The pop-up was below the median on all four inputs, and the $38 acquisition cost is not repaid

claims.claim: Test 3 Funding (✗ Not met): At most $2.5M is left at month 18, against a floor of at least $4.8M
evidence: If losses run at median levels, the cash runs out within the first year

claims.claim: Test 4 Alternatives (✗ Not met): The software business reaches break-even on current cash in about 26 months, and the grocers in its pipeline want fast-delivery tools
Revised answer: No. Do not launch in 2027. Grow the software business, and set measurable triggers for reopening the decision.

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: Quick commerce is growing about 42% a year
no operator makes money from it
evidence: Zipcart (national) $1,200M revenue, −$310M EBITDA, −26% EBITDA margin, −$1.90 contribution / order
QuickBasket (regional) $210M revenue, −$96M EBITDA, −46% margin, −$3.40 contribution / order
EBITDA margin = EBITDA ÷ revenue (e.g., −310 ÷ 1,200 = −25.8%)

claims.claim: the regional operator is pulling back
evidence: QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%) in 2025. It is the closest comparison to a regional newcomer, and it has the worse economics of the two.

claims.claim: ‘Nobody owns the Midwest’ may simply mean nobody has made it pay there yet.
evidence: Zipcart’s one profitable city needed price rises and lost volume as a result (page 9).

claims.claim: Verdict on test 1: half met. The founders are right that demand is growing more than 40% a year. But growth in sales has not produced a pool of profit.
evidence: Every operator in the briefing pack loses money on each order.

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: A dark store loses $6.17 per order at the benchmark median. Only the founders’ plan makes money, and it beats the best observed value on four inputs
evidence: Columbus pop-up (6 weeks): AOV $31, promos 12%, 2.1 orders/rider-hour, 280 orders/day, contribution before site costs −$6.21, site fixed cost/order −$6.36, after site costs −$12.57
Best observed, each input (never seen together): $42, 6%, 3.0, 1,400, +$0.49, −$2.25, −$1.76
Contribution per order = AOV × 27% goods margin + $1.99 delivery fee − $3.10 picking − rider cost ($17.75 ÷ orders per rider-hour) − $1.30 payment and packaging − promotions
Site fixed cost per order = $1.15M a year ÷ (orders per day × 365). For the pop-up, $650k a year

claims.claim: Even at the median, each order loses $2.67 before rent. More volume makes that worse, not better
Best observed values combined still lose $1.76 per order
evidence: At those inputs a site would need 6,387 orders a day to break even, 4.6× the best site seen

claims.claim: At full volume, nine stores would earn +$12M a year on the plan’s inputs and lose $18M at median

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: The plan has no margin for error. Moving any single input back to the benchmark median wipes out 87–136% of its profit per order
evidence: AOV $45 → $34: −$0.73 after change, 136% wiped out
Plan profit = +$2.02 per order. Share wiped out = (plan − after) ÷ plan
Bridge (sequential): +$2.02 → −$2.75 → −$1.36 → −$2.32 → −$1.75 → −$6.17 benchmark median

claims.claim: Every key plan input is outside the observed range
evidence: Order value (AOV): plan $45, best observed $42, +7%
Orders / rider-hour: 3.5 vs 3.0 (top of range), +17%
Orders / site / day: 1,800 vs 1,400 (top of range), +29%
Promotions, % of AOV: 2% vs 6% at every site, −4 pts
The best AOV and best volume come from different sites, and no site achieved both.

claims.claim: AOV is the biggest lever because the goods margin (27%) and promotions both scale with order value.

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: The Columbus pop-up was below the benchmark median on every key input, so there is no evidence yet that Parcelbird runs dark stores better than others
evidence: Order value (AOV): pop-up $31, median $34, plan $45, pop-up vs plan −31%
Promotions, % of AOV: 12%, 6%, 2%, 6× plan
Orders / rider-hour: 2.1, 2.4, 3.5, −40%
Orders / site / day: 280 avg (≈410 in week 6), 900, 1,800, −84% (−77% at exit)
Contribution before site costs: −$6.21, −$2.67, +$3.77
Contribution after site costs: −$12.57, −$6.17, +$2.02
Pop-up site cost per order = $650k ÷ (280 × 365) = $6.36
Week-6 run rate: week-1 orders = 11,800 ÷ Σ1.18^k (k = 0…5) = 1,250; week 6 = 1,250 × 1.18^5 = 2,859 orders, or ≈410 a day.

claims.claim: In fairness to the pop-up: It ran for six weeks from a temporary site, so launch promotions and low volume are to be expected
evidence: Orders grew 18% a week. Even so, the week-6 rate of about 410 a day sits at the bottom of the benchmark range (400–1,400)

claims.claim: Why ‘we run them better’ is unproven
evidence: The 14 benchmark sites already run on Parcelbird software, so the median already includes whatever the software adds
Parcelbird’s own site came in below those customers on every input

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: Customers do not stay long enough to repay the $38 acquisition cost
evidence: 44% of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery ‘at least weekly’ (survey)
22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month 3, at 3.1 orders a month, which is less than once a week
0.22 × 3.1 = 0.68 orders per customer per month from month 3
Founders’ plan: +$3.77 contribution, 10 orders to repay $38, ≈15 months
Best observed: +$0.49, 77 orders, ≈113 months
Median: −$2.67, Never, Never
Pop-up: −$6.21, Never, Never
This assumes no further churn after month 3, so the true figures are worse. Even on the plan’s inputs, repayment takes more than a year.

claims.claim: actual behavior is the more reliable signal
evidence: These are different measures, so they cannot be compared directly.

claims.claim: the plan’s volumes imply about $27M of acquisition spend against a $9.5M budget
evidence: Orders per store per month 1,800 × 365 ÷ 12 = 54,750
Active customers needed ÷ 3.1 orders each = 17,661
Customers to acquire ÷ 22% retained = 80,279
Acquisition cost per store × $38 = $3.05M
Nine stores × 9 = $27.5M
The whole plan budget is $9.5M, including capex and operating losses.
Rough sizing: it ignores orders from customers in months 1–2, which would lower the figure, and churn after month 3, which would raise it.

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: Zipcart’s one profitable city shows what profit costs. Copying its fee and promotion moves would still leave a median Parcelbird site losing $1.05 per order
evidence: Median site today −$6.17; + $3.99 service fee on every order; Promotions 6% → 1% of $34 AOV +$1.70; 14% fewer orders (774/day) −$0.57; Median site with Zipcart’s changes −$1.05
Site cost per order rises from $1.15M ÷ (900 × 365) = $3.50 to $1.15M ÷ (774 × 365) = $4.07.

claims.claim: What Zipcart actually did (shareholder letter)
evidence: Added a $3.99 service fee to every order and cut promotions to 1% of order value
Order volume in that city then fell 14%
Result: +$0.40 contribution per order in its densest city only. Group EBITDA is still −$310M

claims.claim: With Zipcart’s changes, a median site turns positive before site costs (+$3.02 per order)
evidence: Covering site costs as well would take 1,042 orders a day after the volume loss, or 1,211 before it, which is 35% above the median

claims.claim: The founders’ plan assumes promotions of 2% and no service fee, so it does not use this lever
Higher fees work against the impulse, convenience use that quick commerce depends on (uncertainty noted in the briefing pack)

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: Even if everything goes to plan, the launch leaves at most $2.5M by month 18, about half the board’s 12-month runway floor
evidence: Cash today $12.0M; Parcelbird Now spend to month 18 (capex, launch, losses) −$9.5M; Month 18 if $9.5M covers everything $2.5M; Today’s $0.4M/month burn × 18, if not included −$7.2M; Month 18 if it does not −$4.7M
12-month floor at today’s burn: $4.8M
$2.5M ÷ $0.4M a month = about 6 months of runway, against the required 12
At the plan’s own average burn ($9.5M ÷ 18 = $0.53M a month), cash drops below 12 months of runway at around month 11

claims.claim: If unit economics land at the median
evidence: Each store loses $6.17 × 900 × 365 = $2.03M a year at full volume
Nine stores: about $18M a year, 1.5× all the cash Parcelbird has, before any acquisition spend

claims.claim: No fallback funding
evidence: The lead investor says a new round for a delivery operator is ‘unlikely in this market’, so a shortfall cannot be refinanced.

claims.claim: The briefing pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes the existing software burn, so both readings are shown. In the second, cash runs out around month 15 (appendix A2).

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: The software business can break even on today’s cash: about 26 months at 60% growth, with cash bottoming out at $5.4M, above the runway floor throughout
evidence: Cash $7.5M; Low point $5.4M (M25); Break-even ≈ month 26 (monthly burn reaches zero)

Model: cost base implied by today = 81% × $4.1M + $4.8M = $8.1M a year, plus $0.8M of hires = $8.9M, held flat. Revenue = ARR, growing 60% a year, compounded monthly. Monthly burn = (costs − 81% × ARR) ÷ 12. Break-even ARR = $8.9M ÷ 81% = $11.0M.

claims.claim: The path is robust: the floor holds down to about 34% ARR growth, or with costs rising about 10% a year
evidence: 60% ARR growth, flat costs: M26, $5.4M, Yes
50% ARR growth, flat costs: M30, $4.3M, Yes
40% ARR growth, flat costs: M36, $2.7M, Yes
35% ARR growth, flat costs: M40, $1.5M, Yes
30% ARR growth, flat costs: M46, ≈$0M, No, M23
60% growth, costs +10%/yr: M32, $2.8M, Yes
60% growth, costs +15%/yr: M36, $0.9M, No, M19

claims.claim: 60% growth in 2027 means about $2.5M of new ARR, or roughly 26 contracts at $96k
evidence: The 9 late-stage deals cover $0.86M (35%) of that

claims.claim: Hiring can be tied to bookings, so the risk can be managed

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: The pipeline offers a capital-light way into quick commerce: grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, and Parcelbird can sell them the software
evidence: 37 grocers in the software pipeline: 37 × $96k = $3.55M of annual contract value, 87% of today’s ARR
$0.86M of ARR from the 9 late-stage deals (9 × $96k), +21% on today’s $4.1M
≈10 contracts pay for the $0.8M of hires: $0.8M ÷ 81% gross margin = $0.99M ARR, or 10.3 contracts at $96k
81% vs 27%: software gross margin vs. the margin on groceries an operator would earn

claims.claim: Two ways to take part in quick commerce: Operator vs Enabler
evidence: Capital at risk: Operator $5.4M capex plus $1.15M a year of fixed cost per store; $9.5M needed by month 18 / Enabler $0.8M a year of hires, which can be scaled back
Who carries the volume risk: Operator Parcelbird: each store loses money below the required order volume / Enabler The grocer, who uses existing stores with no dark-store rent
Margin: Operator 27% on goods, with negative contribution per order at median inputs / Enabler 81% gross margin on recurring contracts

Fit with customers: Operator Competes for the same delivery customers as the grocers Parcelbird sells to (our inference: a risk to the pipeline) / Enabler Gives the 37 pipeline grocers the fast-delivery offer several of them have asked for
Evidence base: Operator Six-week pop-up, below median on every input / Enabler $4.1M ARR growing 60% a year, plus a named pipeline

claims.claim: A store-based fast-delivery offer still needs product validation with pipeline grocers.

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: Of the four options, only growing the software business meets both of the board’s conditions. Launching or piloting Parcelbird Now fails the runway test
evidence: A. Launch as planned: Profit within current cash? Only if all four inputs beat the best observed; 12 months of runway? No: ≤ $2.5M left at month 18; Upside +$12M a year site contribution on plan inputs; Downside −$18M a year at median inputs; cash runs out; Reversibility Low: $5.4M capex, leases, riders; ✗ Fails

B. One-store pilot: No. One store is not profitable at observed inputs; No: ≈$3.4M cost breaches the floor by month 6; What we learn: mostly already visible from the 14 software sites; −$3.4M; pulls focus from the software; Medium; ✗ Fails

C. Grow the software business and sell fast delivery to grocers: Yes: break-even ≈ month 26 at 60% growth; Yes: low point $5.4M; holds down to ≈34% growth; $3.6M pipeline at 81% gross margin; fast delivery adds to the product; Growth below 34% breaches the floor; hiring can slow to match; High: hiring can be paused; ✓Recommended

D. Status quo: Likely, but more slowly: growth would drop without the hires (not quantified); Yes, if growth holds; Keeps cash; leaves pipeline capacity unused; Competitors serve the grocers who want fast delivery; High; ~ Viable, weaker

claims.claim: The capex and site cost alone ($1.75M) are more than the ≈$1.5M a 12-month pilot could spend without breaching the floor.
evidence: $0.6M capex + $1.15M site cost + 600 orders a day × 365 × $2.67 variable loss ($0.58M) + acquisition to support 600 orders a day ($1.02M) ≈ $3.4M

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: We recommend the board turn down Parcelbird Now for 2027, fund the software plan, and agree the triggers for reopening the question
1 Turn down the Parcelbird Now launch and the one-store pilot for 2027
evidence: Both fail the 12-month runway floor (pages 10 and 13)

claims.claim: 2 Approve $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires
evidence: Pays for itself at about 10 contracts. Release in two tranches tied to bookings

claims.claim: 3 Fund a store-based fast-delivery offer for pipeline grocers
evidence: Validate it with the 9 late-stage grocers before building

claims.claim: 4 Adopt the reopening triggers and a quarterly runway check
evidence: Triggers on page 16. Cash floor = 12 × the latest monthly burn

claims.claim: First 90 days plan
evidence: By end of Jan: Board decision; communicate the reasons to the team and investors — Decision minuted
Feb: Hire tranche 1 (1 engineer, 1 sales). Prioritise closing the 9 late-stage deals — Signed ACV vs. $0.86M
Feb–Mar: Discovery with pipeline grocers on fast delivery from their stores: scope, pricing, pilot customer — ≥ 3 grocers commit to a paid pilot
Mar: Set up a quarterly dashboard: ARR growth, burn, runway, and trigger metrics from the benchmark sites — Dashboard in the board pack
Apr: Release hire tranche 2 if trailing bookings are on track for ≥ 40% ARR growth — Tranche-2 decision
Timing and tranche thresholds are our proposals, not from the pack.

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: The recommendation holds under the main risks. The one that matters most is slower software growth, which hiring discipline can manage
evidence: Software growth slows: 60% ARR growth continues. The floor breaks below ≈34% (flat costs); At 30%: break-even ≈ M46, floor breached at M23; Tranche hires against bookings; review each quarter
Software costs rise: Cost base flat apart from the $0.8M of hires; Costs +15% a year: floor breached at M19; Hold the cost base until break-even
Founders are right about density: The Midwest can reach plan volumes; nobody has shown it yet; Up to +$12M a year site contribution forgone; Triggers keep the option open at no cost
Rider minimum pay: $17.75 an hour today; 2 of the 3 cities are considering minimum pay rules; Each +$1/hr = −$0.42 per order at the median. +$7.06/hr wipes out the plan’s margin; Strengthens the ‘no’
Losing the Midwest to a rival: Being first does not protect profits (QuickBasket is retreating); A rival takes the Midwest market; Sell software to that rival or to grocers instead
Evidence limits: Synthetic data; 6-week pop-up; 14 sites; survey covers ages 25–39 only; Medians could move; Re-run the model each quarter
Model reading of the $9.5M: Generous reading: it includes the existing burn; If it does not, cash runs out ≈ M15; Both readings fail, so the conclusion holds
Rider-cost sensitivity: $1 ÷ 2.4 orders/hr = $0.42 per order; plan margin $2.02 × 3.5 orders/hr = $7.06/hr.

slides.title: 1 MARKET 2 UNIT ECONOMICS 3 FUNDING 4 ALTERNATIVES RECOMMENDATION

claims.claim: Parcelbird Now should come back to the board only if the data show what the plan assumes. Parcelbird already sees most of that data through its software
evidence: All must be met; each maps to one of the four tests
1 Market: An operator reports positive EBITDA in a mid-size US city — Shows a profit pool exists, not just growth — Public operator reporting

2 Unit economics: At least one benchmark site has positive contribution after site costs for 2 consecutive quarters — Today even the best values combined lose $1.76 per order — Parcelbird’s own software data (14+ sites)
2 Customers: Customer payback under 12 months on observed cohorts — Plan inputs give ≈15 months today; needs ≈27% month-3 retention at plan contribution — Customer data from sites on the software
3 Funding: Software at break-even, or ring-fenced outside capital so the floor holds — The floor must hold at all times — Monthly management accounts
Regulation: Rider pay rules settled in the target cities — Each +$1/hr costs $0.42 per order at median productivity — City council decisions
Retention needed = $38 ÷ (12 months × 3.1 orders × $3.77) ≈ 27%.

claims.claim: It can wait for evidence without spending its own capital, and act early if a site proves the economics.
evidence: Parcelbird sees its customers’ dark-store results through its software.

claims.claim: Each order loses money before rent unless AOV, rider productivity and promotions all beat the median
evidence: AOV: Pop-up $31, Median $34, Best observed $42, Plan $45
Gross margin on goods (AOV × 27%): 8.37, 9.18, 11.34, 12.15
+ Delivery fee, net of payment cost: 1.99 each
− Picking and packing labor: −3.10 each
− Rider cost ($17.75 ÷ orders per rider-hour): −8.45, −7.40, −5.92, −5.07
− Payment processing and packaging: −1.30 each
= Contribution before site costs: −6.21, −2.67, 0.49, 3.77
− Site fixed cost ÷ (orders per day × 365): −6.36, −3.50, −2.25, −1.75
= Contribution after site costs, per order: −12.57, −6.17, −1.76, 2.02
Annual result per site at that volume, $M: −1.28, −2.03, −0.90, 1.33
Break-even orders per day = $1.15M ÷ 365 ÷ contribution before site costs: plan 836; best observed 6,387; median never (negative before site costs).

claims.claim: Both readings of the plan and a one-store pilot breach the 12-month floor; the software path does not
evidence: Software path (recommended): Cost base $8.9M a year flat; ARR +60% a year; 81% gross margin; low $5.4M (M25); floor never breached; cash never runs out
Software + one-store pilot: As above + $3.4M spread evenly over months 1–12; $2.0M; M6; Never
Parcelbird Now, reading A: $9.5M covers everything to M18 (generous); $2.5M at M18; ≈M11 at the $0.53M average burn; After M18 unless profitable
Parcelbird Now, reading B: $9.5M evenly over 18 months + existing software burn (no new hires); −$2.5M; M2; ≈M15

claims.claim: Pilot cost build-up (12 months, one Columbus dark store)
evidence: Capex Per the founders’ plan 0.60
Site fixed cost $1.15M a year 1.15
Variable loss 600 orders a day (between the 410 exit rate and the 900 median) × 365 × $2.67 0.58
Customer acquisition 600 × 365 ÷ 12 ÷ 3.1 = 5,887 active ÷ 22% × $38 1.02
Total 3.35

claims.claim: Software model assumptions
evidence: Implied cost base: gross profit 81% × $4.1M = $3.32M; plus $4.8M a year burn = $8.12M a year of operating costs (assumes revenue ≈ ARR)
Add $0.8M a year of hires, giving $8.92M. Held flat in the base case; +10% and +15% a year tested on page 11
ARR compounds monthly at (1 + g)^(1/12). Monthly burn = (costs − 0.81 × ARR) ÷ 12
Runway floor = 12 × that month’s burn. The breach month is the first month cash falls below it
Excludes working capital, one-off costs and any revenue from a fast-delivery offer

claims.claim: Where the pack was silent, we took the reading most favourable to the launch and stress-tested our own alternative. No choice changes the answer
evidence: Contribution per order: Shown both before and after site fixed costs; Founders’ month-18 claim and Zipcart’s figure appear to be before site costs; the median is negative either way
$9.5M and today’s $0.4M/month burn: Showed both readings; led with the generous one; Both fail the runway floor, so the answer does not change
12-month runway floor: 12 × the current month’s net burn; $4.8M at today’s burn; A higher burn raises the floor, so this is the lenient version
Software growth after 2026: 60% continues (stated rate), with cost base flat apart from $0.8M of hires; Stress-tested: the floor holds down to ≈34% growth
Pilot size and cost: One store, 12 months, 600 orders a day, ≈$3.4M; Even capex + site cost alone ($1.75M) exceed the ≈$1.5M a pilot could spend without breaching the floor
Zipcart’s $3.99 fee: Treated as net of payment cost; no change to AOV or rider productivity; Generous to the launch case; the result is still −$1.05 per order
Channel conflict with grocers: Flagged as our inference, not a stated fact; Not needed for the conclusion
Format: Static PDF deck; values printed on charts instead of hover tooltips; Charts use a validated blue/red palette; red = loss, blue = profit

normalized.recommendation: We recommend the board turn down Parcelbird Now for 2027, fund the software plan, and agree the triggers for reopening the question: 1) Turn down the Parcelbird Now launch and the one-store pilot for 2027; 2) Approve $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires (released in two tranches tied to bookings); 3) Fund a store-based fast-delivery offer for pipeline grocers (validate it with the 9 late-stage grocers before building); 4) Adopt the reopening triggers and a quarterly runway check.

alternatives_considered.option: A. Launch as planned (9 stores, 3 cities)
alternatives_considered.treatment: ✗ Fails. Profitable only if all four inputs beat the best observed; ≤ $2.5M left at month 18 vs 12-month runway floor; −$18M a year at median inputs; cash runs out; low reversibility ($5.4M capex, leases, riders).

alternatives_considered.option: B. One-store pilot in Columbus (12 months)
alternatives_considered.treatment: ✗ Fails. One store is not profitable at observed inputs; ≈$3.4M cost breaches the floor by month 6; what we learn is mostly already visible from the 14 software sites; pulls focus from the software.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Grow the software business and sell fast delivery to grocers
alternatives_considered.treatment: ✓ Recommended. Break-even ≈ month 26 at 60% growth; low point $5.4M; holds down to ≈34% growth; $3.6M pipeline at 81% gross margin; high reversibility (hiring can be paused).

alternatives_considered.option: D. Status quo (no launch, no hires)
alternatives_considered.treatment: ~ Viable, weaker. Likely profitable but more slowly: growth would drop without the hires (not quantified); keeps cash but leaves pipeline capacity unused; competitors serve the grocers who want fast delivery.

alternatives_considered.option: Copying Zipcart’s fee and promotion moves ($3.99 service fee, promotions cut to 1%)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Would still leave a median Parcelbird site losing $1.05 per order; higher fees work against impulse, convenience use; founders’ plan does not use this lever.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: All figures from the briefing pack, which contains synthetic data
Software growth slows: 60% ARR growth assumed; the floor breaks below ≈34% (flat costs); at 30% break-even ≈ M46, floor breached at M23
Software costs rise: cost base assumed flat apart from the $0.8M of hires; at +15% a year the floor is breached at M19
Founders are right about density: the Midwest can reach plan volumes; nobody has shown it yet; up to +$12M a year site contribution forgone
Rider minimum pay: $17.75 an hour today; 2 of the 3 cities are considering minimum pay rules; each +$1/hr = −$0.42 per order at the median; +$7.06/hr wipes out the plan’s margin
Losing the Midwest to a rival: being first does not protect profits (QuickBasket is retreating)
Evidence limits: synthetic data; 6-week pop-up; 14 sites; survey covers ages 25–39 only; medians could move
The briefing pack does not say whether the $9.5M includes the existing software burn; generous reading used; if it does not, cash runs out ≈ M15
Customer repayment months assume no further churn after month 3, so the true figures are worse
Acquisition spend sizing is rough: ignores orders from customers in months 1–2 (would lower) and churn after month 3 (would raise)
Zipcart fee analysis uses generous assumptions: fee taken as net of payment costs, AOV and rider productivity unchanged after volume loss
Higher fees work against impulse, convenience use (uncertainty noted in the briefing pack)
Channel conflict with grocers is our inference, not a stated fact
A store-based fast-delivery offer still needs product validation with pipeline grocers
Software model is simplified: assumes revenue ≈ ARR; excludes working capital, one-off costs and any revenue from a fast-delivery offer
Runway floor measured as 12 × the current month’s net burn ($4.8M at today’s burn), the lenient version
Contribution per order shown both before and after site fixed costs; founders’ month-18 claim and Zipcart’s figure appear to be before site costs
Status quo growth drop without the hires is not quantified
Timing and tranche thresholds are our proposals, not from the pack
next_steps: By end of Jan: Board decision; communicate the reasons to the team and investors (measure: decision minuted)
Feb: Hire tranche 1 (1 engineer, 1 sales). Prioritise closing the 9 late-stage deals (measure: signed ACV vs. $0.86M)
Feb–Mar: Discovery with pipeline grocers on fast delivery from their stores: scope, pricing, pilot customer (measure: ≥ 3 grocers commit to a paid pilot)
Mar: Set up a quarterly dashboard: ARR growth, burn, runway, and trigger metrics from the benchmark sites (measure: dashboard in the board pack)
Apr: Release hire tranche 2 if trailing bookings are on track for ≥ 40% ARR growth (measure: tranche-2 decision)

Reopen the operator decision only if all triggers are met: an operator reports positive EBITDA in a mid-size US city; at least one benchmark site has positive contribution after site costs for 2 consecutive quarters; customer payback under 12 months on observed cohorts; software at break-even or ring-fenced outside capital so the floor holds; rider pay rules settled in the target cities
